newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Parched Welsh drinkers set for "wet" Sundays.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Parched Welsh drinkers set for "wet" Sundays.

text.p: Drinkers in this Welsh village have not been able to have a beer at their favourite pub on a Sunday for more than 100 years.
But on Wednesday, if the prayers of the thirsty are answered, the whole of Wales will be allowed to drink on the Sabbath.

Porthmadog and several villages on the windswept Lleyn peninsula, a finger of land that juts out from the west coast of Wales, have been "dry" on Sundays since 1881 because of a law passed by the parliament in London.
On Wednesday, locals are expected to vote overwhelmingly in favour of allowing pubs and hotels to serve alcohol on Sundays.

"There is little doubt that the vote will be in favour of allowing people to enjoy a drink on a Sunday," David Baird-Murray, chairman of the pressure group, the Seven Day Opening Council, told Reuters.
"Some people are worried the community will lose part of its Welshness -- its national identity. But this is not about being Welsh," he said. "This is about having a choice."
Since parliament passed the Sunday Closing Wales Act in 1881, it has been illegal to sell alcohol in around 70 "licensed" premises in the area on a Sunday.
Supermarkets are also not allowed to sell alcohol and hotels cannot serve even a glass of wine with a meal.
Baird-Murray, who has been a hotelier in the area for 45 of his 65 years, has been fighting the law for nearly four decades and during that time has seen most counties across Wales go "wet".
For 80 years pubs throughout Wales were shut on Sunday but in 1961 the Welsh were given the opportunity to vote, county by county, on whether to repeal the law in their local communities.

There have been five such ballots since 1961, and one by one, counties across Wales voted to go wet -- with the exception of the Lleyn peninsula, which is now the only area in all of Europe where pubs have to close on Sundays.
According to Baird-Murray, the original Act was passed, "in the dead of the night" by ultra-religious Welsh members of parliament after most of the members had gone home.
Welsh miners, throats parched by six days of coal dust, were undeterred by the law and travelled on Sundays, usually their only day off, to the neighbouring border county of Monmouthshire for a pint.

But during World War One, when many miners consistently failed to return home in time for their Monday shifts, the government stopped Sunday drinking in Monmouthshire by passing the "Defence of the Realm Act of 1915".
"The government thought the miners' drinking was harming the war effort," Baird-Murray said.
That law was swept aside after the war but the conservative people of Llyen, where Welsh and not English is the predominate language, have stubbornly kept their area an alcohol-free zone on Sundays.

"The resistance has come from a small but well-organised religious faction," Baird-Murray said. But religious zeal will not be able to stem the tide of change that is set to wash over "dry" Porthmadog on Wednesday, he believes.

Due to electoral boundary changes the Llyen peninsula has been incorporated into a larger new county called Gwynedd. In past ballots, the majority of the Gwynedd electorate have voted in favour of Sunday drinking, Baird-Murray said.
Publicans and hoteliers in Porthmadog are not taking anything for granted, however. Pubs, hotels, and shops are adorned with signs encouraging people to vote "Yes".
"The enemy this time is apathy. The only worry is that people in favour won't get out to vote," said Robert Jones, owner of the Ship hotel, bar and restaurant.

Jones said that during the height of the summer tourist season, Porthmadog becomes a virtual ghost town as holidaymakers join a mass exodus to the "wet" village of Pernrhyndeudraeth, only a few miles (km) away.
"You have to see it to believe it. People in taxis, cars, coaches, and mini-buses leaving town to just go across the river. The pubs on the other side are just packed with people," he lamented.
"I can't put an exact figure on it, but I've lost a lot of money not being allowed to open on Sundays."
The Seven Day Opening Council estimates that pubs and hotels will see their takings increase by up to 25 percent once they are allowed to open on Sundays.
Provided the vote is "Yes", the Ship will be open on Sunday, November 10 and the first 20 pints of beer it serves on that day will be free, Jones said.
"That's the first 20 pints in total -- not first 20 pints for each customer," Jones added. He reckons that after a 115-year wait, some of the locals may be thirsty.
